Feser’s precise name for the Unmoved Mover: something that actualizes other things without being actualized — pure actuality.

flashcards.front: Does the argument need a beginning of the universe?
flashcards.back: No. Feser grants a possibly infinite past, as Aristotle believed; the argument is about what sustains things now.

flashcards.front: Does the argument assume the universe as a whole has a cause?
flashcards.back: No. It starts from any single thing. Applying the result to everything is a consequence, not a premise.
Only what goes from potential to actual needs a cause. Pure act has no potential, so it neither needs nor could have one.

flashcards.front: Triangle analogy (against the ‘no real difference’ rejoinder)
flashcards.back: Equating ‘whatever goes from potency to act has a cause’ with ‘everything has a cause’ is like equating ‘all triangles have three sides’ with ‘all figures have three sides’.

flashcards.front: Three replies to the ‘ad hoc’ charge
flashcards.back: (1) Motives cannot make a claim false — that is ad hominem. (2) It is historically false: the claim has been put this way since Aristotle. (3) It follows from the analysis of change anyway.
Conceiving A without conceiving B is not the same as conceiving A existing without B (trilateral and triangle; a man without a height).
What makes a sudden appearance a coming-into-existence rather than a transportation? Only the kind of cause — so causation sneaks back in.
We learn geometry from black-ink diagrams, yet it applies to figures of any colour; likewise causality applies wherever there is potential, observed or not.
If the principle of causality were false, things could pop into existence anywhere at any time — and they do not.
Proves too much (Schaffer); particles have dispositions (Martin); other sciences and naturalism rely on causation; physics is not exhaustive (the later Russell).

flashcards.front: Metal detector, the easy-A student, the drunk under the streetlamp
flashcards.back: A method’s success with what it is built to find tells you nothing about what it cannot detect.
It concerns events in time, not existence; laws presuppose natures; and mathematical physics assumes inertia rather than proving it (Weisheipl).

flashcards.front: Two replies on the block universe
flashcards.back: (1) Denying all change is incoherent — science rests on changing experiences (Healey). (2) The block’s own existence would still need an actualizer.
A cause must make its effect intelligible, not necessary. Indeterministic causation is still causation.
Absence from a representation is not a representation of absence — and in a colour hold the lines even let you infer the contour that only colour will supply.
Quantum: potentiality with nothing shown actualizing it — Heisenberg called the probabilities ‘potentia’. Block universe: actuality with no potentiality. Either way causation drops out.
Formal (its nature, grounding the probability); efficient (whatever generated it); deeper efficient (whatever keeps it in existence now).
If indeterministic links were not causal, I would not be responsible for your radiation sickness — which is absurd.
Whatever is in an effect is in its cause formally, virtually or eminently; a cause cannot give what it does not have.
Twenty in the wallet / credit in the bank / the power to print twenties.
Grasping universal concepts, combining them into thoughts, and reasoning from thought to thought. The first is the most fundamental.

flashcards.front: Why only one purely actual being?
flashcards.back: Differentiating two would need some feature or privation one lacks — that is, an unactualized potential, which pure act cannot have.

flashcards.front: Unmoved vs. unmovable: the three-way dilemma
flashcards.back: A potential in the first actualizer would be actualized by (1) something else — so it is not first; (2) a purely actual part — so that part is first; (3) a mixed part — so the regress restarts.

flashcards.front: Fallacy of accident (in the unmovable-mover section)
flashcards.back: Inferring that all actualizers must change because the observed ones do — like concluding that no seven-footer could be president.
Any change presupposes a substance that undergoes it: there is no cooling without something that cools.

flashcards.front: What does step 7 claim, and why?
flashcards.back: A substance’s existence at any moment requires its potential for existence to be actualized at that moment — its matter could have been otherwise.

flashcards.front: Steps 9–10: the two options for the actualizer A
flashcards.back: Either A’s own existence is being actualized, starting a regress of concurrent actualizers, or A is purely actual.

flashcards.front: What does step 11 claim, and why?
flashcards.back: A regress of concurrent actualizers is hierarchical and so cannot be infinite, because borrowed power needs an unborrowed source.
Whatever exists in time can change; pure act cannot change; so it exists outside time.
Being material entails being changeable and in time, so pure act is immaterial and therefore incorporeal.
Every actualization comes from pure act directly or through a series ending in it — so all power derives from it (omnipotence).
Forms exist either concretely in things or abstractly in an intellect; they cannot be in pure act concretely, so they are there as in an intellect.
For there to be a single purely actual cause with these attributes just is for God to exist.

flashcards.front: Objection: ‘a first cause isn’t God’ → reply
flashcards.back: Stage 2 derives the divine attributes from pure actuality alone, so the argument reaches far more than a bare cause.
No premise concerns the universe as a whole; the argument starts from any single thing.
Particles describe the mechanism of support, not a refutation of it — and no one raises this against engineers or doctors.

flashcards.front: Objection: there are no simultaneous causes → reply
flashcards.back: Simultaneous does not mean instantaneous: an immediate cause and its effect are one event, however long it lasts.

flashcards.front: Objection: infinite series cannot be ruled out (Oppy) → reply
flashcards.back: Aristotelians reject only a series of instruments with no source of power; mathematical series involve no instrumental causes at all.

flashcards.front: Objection: calling causes ‘instrumental’ begs the question (Sobel) → reply
flashcards.back: ‘Instrumental’ means only ‘derives its power from another’; that the regress must end is then argued, not assumed.

flashcards.front: Objection: a purely actual actualizer is incoherent → reply
flashcards.back: The objection begs the question, commits a fallacy of accident, and points to no contradiction of the ‘immortal mortal’ kind.
The refuted theses (geocentrism, natural place) are scientific; act and potency is metaphysics, which science presupposes.

flashcards.front: Distinction: cause of becoming vs. cause of being
flashcards.back: Becoming: what originally produced a thing (the brewing). Being: what keeps it in existence now. The argument concerns being.
Privation is lacking what your nature requires (a blind dog). Negation is lacking what is not proper to you (a stone’s lack of sight).
Pure act is uncaused, since there is nothing in it to actualize — not self-caused, which would require existing before itself.
Prime matter depends on form and form on matter, so the composite would be an explanatory circle unless something outside it holds it in being.

flashcards.front: Why ‘chemical bonding’ doesn’t answer what keeps water in existence
flashcards.back: It restates the question: the atoms could be bonded otherwise, so why this way, now? Appealing to atomic structure only pushes it down a level.

errors_fixed: keyTerms/Intellect: origin gave 'intus legere (to read within)' as the etymology of intellectus. That is a medieval gloss, not the derivation (intellegere). Reworded to say so.

keyTerms/Inference to the best explanation: origin credited the name to C. S. Peirce ('abduction'). The name is Gilbert Harman's (1965); Peirce's abduction is a near relative, not the same coinage. Corrected.

keyTerms/Uncaused cause: origin gave a scholastic Latin phrase 'causa incausata' that is not a standard term. Term cut; its one real contribution (uncaused vs. self-caused / causa sui) folded into Pure actuality's confuseWith, with no invented Latin.

keyTerms/Divine simplicity: origin glossed simplicitas as 'without folds'. Term cut (the chapter defers simplicity to later chapters); the contrast survives in Unity (divine) without the shaky etymology.
keyTerms/Special pleading: origin claimed the legal 'special plea' 'introduced new matter to evade the main issue'. Replaced with a safer account of the legal-to-informal shift.
keyTerms/Formally / virtually / eminently: origin said the triad is 'also used by Descartes'. Descartes uses the formal/eminent pair (Meditation III), not the three-way scholastic set. Narrowed.

keyTerms/Problem of evil: origin ran 'goes back to Epicurus as reported by Lactantius' as settled attribution, and the topic is never discussed in Chapter 1. Term cut; the metaphysical-versus-moral goodness point kept in Goodness (in the general sense).
